publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Racialized Campaign Ads: The Emotional Content in Implicit Racial Appeals Primes White Racial Attitudes

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We contend that racial priming is most effective when an IRA arouses anger.

span.label: racial priming by implicit racial appeals
span.quote: Our theory suggests that anger and fear, in the context of an implicit racial appeal, influence whites’ views about race differently.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Using an experiment over two waves, we induce anger and fear from an implicit racialized campaign ad and find that anger uniquely boosts opposition to racial policies among white racial conservatives.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: anger and symbolic racism are stored as tightly linked associations in memory, so arousing anger activates the racial belief system and makes it available for the subsequent policy judgement
span.quote: We argue that anger and symbolic racism (SR) are tightly linked in memory, and evoking this emotion in the context of an IRA should then activate this belief system and cause a shift in opposition to racial policies.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: emotional (mood-congruent) priming: being returned to the emotional state in which an attitude was learned makes that attitude easier to recall
span.quote: We rely on Bower and Forgas’s (2001) theory of emotional priming to argue that specific emotions from IRAs play an important role in activating racial attitudes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: because contemporary racial discourse is dominated by blame attribution, and blame is the appraisal that produces anger, anger rather than fear is the emotion bonded to whites' racial predispositions
span.quote: If contemporary discussions about race are dominated by blame rhetoric, we suspect that anger should be strongly linked to whites’ negative racial predispositions.

span.label: The sample was a non-representative convenience sample of undergraduates, over-weighted toward liberals.
span.quote: The sample reflects one of convenience—undergraduate students—and is not representative of the U.S. population as a whole.

span.label: It is unknown whether an adult sample would show the same effect.
span.quote: First, it is unclear whether an adult sample would produce similar findings.

span.label: Generalisation beyond crime to other racialised issue domains is untested.
span.quote: Second, it is unclear whether our results are generalizable to other domains associated with race like affirmative action or welfare.

span.label: the paper takes Bower and Forgas's theory of emotional priming — a psychological account of mood-congruent recall — and uses it as the explanatory engine for a political-communication effect
span.quote: We rely on Bower and Forgas’s (2001) theory of emotional priming to argue that specific emotions from IRAs play an important role in activating racial attitudes.

span.label: anger
span.quote: We suspect this effect occurs because anger and whites’ negative racial attitudes are tightly linked in memory

span.label: fear
span.quote: Our theory suggests that anger and fear, in the context of an implicit racial appeal, influence whites’ views about race differently

span.label: racial priming
span.quote: Most of the research on racial priming seems to conflate the effect of negative emotions

span.label: racial attitudes
span.quote: We suspect this effect occurs because anger and whites’ negative racial attitudes are tightly linked in memory

span.label: racial conservatives
span.quote: While racial conservatives find fault in the moral character of blacks, racial liberals blame the racism and discrimination that blacks have endured over the years

span.label: racial liberals
span.quote: While racial conservatives find fault in the moral character of blacks, racial liberals blame the racism and discrimination that blacks have endured over the years

span.label: negative emotion, as this paper refuses to use it - the charge is CONFLATION: most research on racial priming treats negative affect as one thing, and the paper's contribution is to show that two negative emotions from the same advertisement do different work. A category being used where a distinction was needed
span.quote: Most of the research on racial priming seems to conflate the effect of negative emotions

span.label: anger, in this account - not a stronger version of negative feeling but a SPECIFIC ROUTE: it is argued to be tightly linked in memory to whites' negative racial attitudes, so it reaches them where another negative emotion may not. The claim is about association, not intensity
span.quote: We suspect this effect occurs because anger and whites’ negative racial attitudes are tightly linked in memory

span.label: racial conservative and racial liberal, as defined here by WHERE THEY LOCATE THE CAUSE: conservatives find fault in the moral character of blacks, liberals blame the racism and discrimination endured. The two are separated by an attribution rather than by a policy position, which is what lets one emotion move them in opposite directions
span.quote: While racial conservatives find fault in the moral character of blacks, racial liberals blame the racism and discrimination that blacks have endured over the years

span.label: builds-on → Bower and Forgas (2001)
span.quote: We rely on Bower and Forgas’s (2001) theory of emotional priming to argue that specific emotions from IRAs play an important role in activating racial attitudes.

span.label: builds-on → Banks and Valentino (2012)
span.quote: In fact, Banks and Valentino (2012) observe such an effect; they find that anger (independent of racial or political content), and not disgust or fear, is highly correlated with, and can in fact activate, SR.

span.label: replicates → Banks and Valentino (2012)
span.quote: However, Banks and Valentino (2012) find similar results on an adult national sample.

span.label: anger —distinct-from→ fear
span.note: differs in: WHICH ONE IS BOUND TO RACIAL ATTITUDES IN MEMORY - the paper's claim is that they are not interchangeable negatives, and that the difference is associative rather than a matter of degree · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE DISTINCTION THE PAPER EXISTS TO DRAW, and it is drawn against its own field: the charge is that research on racial priming conflates the two under `negative emotion`.
span.quote: Our theory suggests that anger and fear, in the context of an implicit racial appeal, influence whites’ views about race differently

span.label: anger —causes→ racial attitudes
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — Hedged as a suspicion - `we suspect this effect occurs because` - and weighted for it. The mechanism is associative access, so what the emotion does is REACH the attitude, not strengthen it.
span.quote: We suspect this effect occurs because anger and whites’ negative racial attitudes are tightly linked in memory

span.label: racial conservatives —contrasted-with→ racial liberals
span.note: differs in: WHERE EACH LOCATES THE CAUSE of black disadvantage - in moral character, or in racism and discrimination endured. An attributional difference, not a policy one · strength of the relation: 0.9 — Recorded because the paper's headline result depends on it: the same anger, from the same advertisement, moves these two groups in OPPOSITE directions on the same policies.
span.quote: While racial conservatives find fault in the moral character of blacks, racial liberals blame the racism and discrimination that blacks have endured over the years

span.label: regression
span.quote: Note.—Entries are unstandardized OLS regression coefficients, and the standard errors are in parentheses.

span.label: interaction term in linear regression
span.quote: If so, we expect a positive and significant interaction between the anger condition and SR in linear regressions.

span.label: Cronbach's alpha (intercoder/scale reliability)
span.quote: Cronbach’s alpha reveals a high level of reliability across the two coders—fear (.89) and anger (.85).

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: Given our small sample size, we also use bootstrapping to reestimate our standard errors from column 1.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: The figure displays a 95-percent confidence interval around the marginal effect of anger.

span.label: An implicit racial appeal that arouses anger significantly amplifies the effect of symbolic racism on opposition to racial policies among whites.
span.quote: The interaction between the anger condition and SR is positive, substantively large, and statistically significant.

span.label: An implicit racial appeal that arouses fear does not amplify the effect of symbolic racism, so the priming effect is specific to anger rather than to negative emotion in general.
span.quote: Conversely, the fear condition does not boost the effect of SR on racial policy opinions.

span.label: Among whites low in symbolic racism, anger moved policy opinion in the opposite direction, making racial liberals more supportive of racial policies.
span.quote: Looking at whites low in SR, we find that the effect of anger is negative and significant. This result suggests that anger also motivates racial liberals to be more supportive of racial policies.

span.label: The marginal effect of anger on racial policy opinion grows monotonically with symbolic racism while the marginal effect of fear stays flat across the same range.
span.quote: As we suspect, the marginal effect of anger on racial policy opinions increases as SR increases. The marginal effect of fear is relatively flat across levels of SR.

span.label: The emotion manipulation worked: open-ended responses in the anger ad condition showed significantly more intense anger than both the control and the fear conditions.
span.quote: Participants in the anger condition expressed significantly more intense anger relative to subjects in the control condition (β = .44; p ≥ .001) and respondents in the fear condition (β = .34; p ≥ .001).

span.label: Overall, the experiment shows anger is the emotional channel through which an implicit racial appeal primes symbolic racism.
span.quote: In summary, our experimental results show that anger from an IRA primes SR, while fear has no effect on SR.

span.label: implicit racial appeal (IRA)
span.quote: An IRA appears in a nonracial manner; it omits racial nouns or adjectives such as “black” or “racial” and instead consists of negative images of blacks (Mendelberg 2001).

span.label: symbolic racism (SR)
span.quote: Sears and Kinder define this belief system as an amalgam of anti-black affect and a violation of core American values like individual initiative.

span.label: racial priming
span.quote: Mendelberg (2001) characterizes racial priming as a political appeal wherein a message’s racial content is unrecognized by the audience, thereby allowing the cue to effectively activate whites’ racial attitudes.

span.label: appraisal theory of emotion
span.quote: The appraisal theory of emotion allows scholars to differentiate between discrete emotions and understand their likely antecedents and consequences.

span.label: anger (as distinguished from fear by its appraisals)
span.term: anger (as distinguished from fear by its appraisals)
span.quote: People experience anger when they feel threatened and are certain who is blameworthy for the threatening action (Lazarus 1991).

span.label: emotional condition of the ad (anger vs fear vs control)
span.term: emotional condition of the ad (anger vs fear vs control)
span.quote: Anger and Fear are dummy variables, where 1 = if they were in the treatment condition and 0 = if they were in the control condition.

span.label: symbolic racism (pretest racial predisposition)
span.quote: In our model, we regressed Racial Policy Opinions on emotion dummies (Anger and Fear), SR, and the interaction between the two, controlling for Gender and Age.

span.label: racial policy opinions (opposition to racial policies)
span.term: racial policy opinions (opposition to racial policies)
span.quote: Racial Policy Opinions ranges from 0 to 1, where the higher value corresponds with the more conservative response.

span.label: age
span.quote: Age is a continuous variable and ranges from 18 to 38 years old.

span.label: 113 — total number of experimental subjects in wave 2, of whom 85 were white
span.quote: Our total sample size was 113 and included 85 whites.

span.label: 65 percent — share of the student sample who were liberals (a stated limitation of the convenience sample)
span.quote: We obtained good variation on gender (47-percent male), but liberals were overrepresented in the sample (65 percent).

span.label: 59 percent — retention/response rate from wave 1 (190 subjects) to wave 2
span.quote: Wave 1 had 190 subjects, while 113 participated in wave 2. Our response rate was 59 percent.

span.label: β = .44; p ≥ .001 — intensity of expressed anger in the anger-ad condition relative to control, in the manipulation check
span.quote: Participants in the anger condition expressed significantly more intense anger relative to subjects in the control condition (β = .44; p ≥ .001) and respondents in the fear condition (β = .34; p ≥ .001).

span.label: β = .57; p ≥ .001 — intensity of expressed fear in the fear-ad condition relative to control
span.quote: In the fear condition, respondents expressed an intense amount of fear (β = .57; p ≥ .001) relative to the control group.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1093/poq/nft010.
